what_it_does: Running a large language model on a GPU is slowed by the sheer volume of data that must be fetched from the high-bandwidth memory chips on the GPU card. Ecco compresses that data by 4× before it is stored in those chips, and decompresses it at full speed on the way back in, making the GPU's memory effectively 4× larger and 4× faster without changing how the model works.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A GPU's large memory pool (called HBM — a stack of fast DRAM chips bonded to the chip) is the bottleneck during language model inference: the model's billions of weights and the key-value cache (the running record of past token representations) must be fetched every token step, yet arithmetic units often sit waiting. If the data were compressed, fewer bytes would need to travel, freeing that bottleneck.

How it works. Ecco places a compressor and a decompressor in hardware between the GPU's on-chip cache (L2) and the HBM. Data is always stored compressed in HBM and decompressed on the way to the compute cores.

For weights and the key-value cache (targeting 4× compression): the tensor is divided into groups of 128 numbers. Each group is matched against one of 64 pre-learned 'pattern' sets — each pattern is a set of 15 representative values discovered offline by a clustering algorithm (k-means) that partitions similar groups together. The closest pattern is chosen, and each number in the group is replaced by an index (0–15) pointing to its nearest representative value. Those indices are then Huffman-coded — a scheme that assigns shorter bit-strings to more common indices, with the best of 4 pre-built codebooks selected per group. Outlier values that would otherwise be lost are padded in using spare bits.

For activations (intermediate values the model computes during a forward pass), a simpler uniform scheme targets 2× compression.

The key design choice. Huffman decoding is normally sequential and slow. Ecco's decompressor instead runs 64 parallel Huffman decoders simultaneously on overlapping 15-bit windows of the compressed block. Their outputs are merged in a six-stage tree-shaped combiner, with 128 parallel mappers finishing the translation from index to actual float value. This makes decompression fast enough to keep pace with the L2 cache.

The result. Ecco achieves up to 2.9× speedup over the AWQ quantization framework and 2.4× over the Olive accelerator, while expanding effective memory capacity by nearly 4×, all with accuracy matching or beating these baselines on LLaMA and Mistral models.
